sections.name: File setup (part 1)
sections.title: Search settings for each data file
sections.what: Maps each search area, such as styles, colors, charts, fonts, icons, motion and UX guidelines, to its data file. For each area it lists the columns that are searched and the columns shown in results.
sections.why: Likely reason: keeping these lists in one place means a new area needs only one new entry.
sections.watch_out: Column names must match the CSV header text exactly, including spaces and symbols, or the search and results will not work for that column.

sections.name: File setup (part 2)
sections.title: Columns shown in full and stack settings
sections.what: Lists the columns whose text is never cut short, such as code snippets and checklists, and the list of framework stacks, each tied to its own data file. Also sets the shared columns used by all stacks.
sections.why: Likely reason: cutting a code snippet in the middle would make it unusable, so those columns are kept whole.
sections.watch_out: A new code-style column must be added to the never-cut list, or it may be shortened in results.

sections.name: File setup (part 3)
sections.title: Word splitting and filler word list
sections.what: Breaks text into lowercase words, removes punctuation and drops words shorter than two letters and common filler words like the and is. Short technical words like ui, css and 3d are kept.
sections.why: The code comment says short domain words must stay searchable, so filtering is by a list rather than by length alone.
sections.watch_out: Single-letter words are always dropped, so a one-letter search term finds nothing.

sections.name: _normalize
sections.title: Replacing spelling variants before search
sections.what: Swaps common spelling variants and shortcuts, such as colour to color, a11y to accessibility, and dark-mode to dark, so different spellings match the same content.
sections.why: Likely reason: users get the same results whichever spelling they type.
sections.watch_out: The swap is plain text replacement, so the shortcut nav also changes inside longer words such as navigation, which garbles them.

sections.name: BM25 (part 1)
sections.title: Building the word index
sections.what: Turns a list of documents into a searchable index. It counts the words in each document, counts how many documents each word appears in, and gives each word a rarity score.
sections.why: This is the setup step that the ranking needs before it can score matches.
sections.watch_out: Calling the index build again on the same object adds counts on top of the old ones, so a new object should be created instead.

sections.name: BM25: score
sections.title: Scoring documents against a query
sections.what: For each document, adds up a relevance score for every query word it contains. Rare words and words that appear often in a short document count for more. Returns every document with its score, best match first.
sections.why: Likely reason: this is the standard BM25 ranking, a common method for text search.
sections.watch_out: Every document is scored on each search, so searches slow down as the data grows, which is acceptable for these small files.

sections.name: _load_csv
sections.title: Loading a CSV file with a cache
sections.what: Reads a CSV file into rows and remembers the result. If the file's modified time has not changed, the saved rows are returned without reading the file again.
sections.why: The comment says the same files are reused across several searches in one run, so caching saves time.
sections.watch_out: A missing file raises an error here, and nothing in this section catches it, so the search stops.

sections.name: _get_bm25
sections.title: Remembering the search index per file
sections.what: Builds the word-matching index for a data file and reuses it until that file changes on disk. Users notice repeated searches responding faster.
sections.why: Likely reason: rebuilding the index on every search would be slow for files with many rows.
sections.watch_out: The cache is keyed on the file's modification time, so an edit that does not change that timestamp could be missed.

sections.name: _search_csv
sections.title: Running one search over one data file
sections.what: Reads a data file, scores each row against the query, and returns the top matching rows with only the chosen columns. A missing or unreadable file returns an empty result or a row containing an error message.
sections.why: Shared engine so every search area gets the same ranking and error handling.
sections.watch_out: Read errors come back as a fake result row with an _error key, so callers must check for it or it will look like a normal hit.

sections.name: _suggest_terms
sections.title: Offering near-miss words after no hits
sections.what: When a search finds nothing, proposes up to six known vocabulary words that share a short beginning with the query, so the user can retry with a better word.
sections.why: The docstring states the purpose: so the caller can retry instead of silently reporting nothing.
sections.watch_out: Matching uses only the first three letters, so suggestions can be loosely related. The comment about sorting by frequency does not match the code, which keeps discovery order.

sections.name: _load_product_keywords
sections.title: Loading product keywords from the data file
sections.what: Reads keywords from the product data file and merges them with a short built-in list, longest first, so product types are detected from current data.
sections.why: The comment says this keeps the list in sync with the data and avoids manual edits. The built-in list is a fallback when the data folder is missing.
sections.watch_out: If the file is missing or unreadable, the function silently falls back to the short built-in list with no warning.

sections.name: _domain_keywords
sections.title: Keyword lists for each search area
sections.what: Holds the words that signal each area, such as colour, chart, or animation. The table is built once on first use and reused after that.
sections.why: Likely reason: keeps all routing vocabulary in one place and avoids rebuilding it on every search.
sections.watch_out: Some words such as font and typography appear in more than one area, so editing this table can change which area wins for a query.

sections.name: detect_domain
sections.title: Picking the right search area for a query
sections.what: Scores every area by how many of its keywords appear in the query, giving longer phrases more weight, and returns the best one. If nothing matches, it falls back to the style area.
sections.why: The docstring says longer phrases are more specific. A fixed tie order keeps results the same on every run.
sections.watch_out: Keywords containing symbols such as the hash sign sit at word edges where the boundary check may not match as a person expects.

sections.name: search
sections.title: Main search entry for one area
sections.what: Runs a search in one area. If no area is given, it detects one first, then returns the results plus the detected area and a runner-up area. Empty results include suggested words.
sections.why: This is the public search that the rest of the skill calls.
sections.watch_out: An unknown area name silently falls back to the style settings instead of reporting an error.

sections.name: search_stack
sections.title: Searching a specific tech stack
sections.what: Searches the guidance file for one named framework and returns matches. An unknown stack name returns an error listing the stacks that exist.
sections.why: Each stack has its own guidance file, so advice stays framework-specific.
sections.watch_out: All stacks share the same column settings, so the stack name only chooses the file, not which columns are searched.

summary: Search engine core that ranks rows from CSV style-guide data files by relevance to a text query, using the BM25 method. Only part of the file was available for this review.
purpose: Lets the design tools find the most relevant guidance rows for a user's words, such as colors, fonts, charts or specific frameworks.
why: Likely reason: ranking by relevance gives useful results from plain text, and caching avoids reading the same file again in one run. Reason for some choices not stated in the code.
how: First, the search settings say which file and columns belong to each area. Text is lowercased, common spelling variants are swapped, punctuation is removed and filler words are dropped. A word index is built from the rows, and each row is scored against the query. Loaded CSV files are remembered and reloaded only when their modification time changes.
inputs: A search area name, a query text, and the CSV data files in the data folder.
outputs: Ranked rows from the CSV files and the relevance order. The shown sections include the ranking and the loaded rows; the rest of the search flow is not visible.
risks: Column names must match CSV headers exactly. Calling the index build twice on one object adds counts on top of the old ones. A missing data file stops the load with an error. The spelling swap can garble longer words that contain a shortcut.
debug: If a search returns nothing, check the word list and column names for that area against the CSV header row. If an area fails to load, confirm its file exists in the data folder. If results look skewed, check that each search creates a fresh index object.
